Xavi Simons’ season, and indeed his World Cup dreams, have been cruelly truncated after the Tottenham midfielder suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament in Saturday’s 1-0 win over Wolves. The 23-year-old was stretchered off the pitch in the 63rd minute, his despairing expression a testament to the severity of the injury. Scans have since confirmed that the Netherlands international will be out for around eight months, a blow that will not only impact his club’s Premier League survival bid but also the Oranje’s chances at the World Cup finals this summer.

item.title: Xavi Simons ruled out of rest of season and World Cup with ruptured ACL
item.description:
Tragic Blow to Tottenham and Netherlands: Xavi Simons’ Season and World Cup Hopes Shattered

Xavi Simons’ world came crashing down in the 63rd minute at Molineux on Saturday, as the Tottenham midfielder’s anterior cruciate ligament gave way, ending his season and all but ruling him out of the World Cup finals for the Netherlands this summer. The devastating news has cast a pall of despair over Spurs, who were struggling to stay afloat in the Premier League, and Simons, who had been instrumental in the team’s creative play. The 23-year-old’s injury, confirmed by scans, means he will be sidelined for approximately eight months, a cruel twist of fate that has left him, and the football world, reeling.

item.title: Liverpool up to fourth but Salah injured in eventful Palace win
item.description:
A Flicker of Hope for Liverpool as Palace Win Comes at a Cost

The lights have flickered back on at Anfield, and Liverpool’s beleaguered fans can momentarily breathe a sigh of relief. A 3-1 victory over Crystal Palace has propelled the Reds up to fourth in the Premier League, but the sweet taste of success is tempered by the devastating news that star forward Mohamed Salah may have played his final game for the club. As the Egyptian international limped off the pitch with a worrying knee injury, the collective heart of the Liverpool faithful sank. The question on everyone’s lips is: what now for the Reds?

item.title: MK Dons seal promotion to League One
item.description:
Football’s Unlikely Hero: MK Dons Rise to Prominence in League One

The final whistle at Stadium MK sent shockwaves through the English football landscape as MK Dons sealed promotion to League One with a resounding 3-0 victory over Tranmere on a damp spring evening. The triumph marked a triumphant conclusion to a season that has been anything but straightforward for Paul Tisdale’s men, who have defied expectations to secure a spot in the third tier of English football. As the jubilant MK Dons faithful erupted into a frenzy of noise and colour, the reality of their achievement began to sink in – a remarkable turn of events that has catapulted this small-town club into the spotlight.

item.title: How to Reduce the Environmental Impact of Collecting
item.description:
The Weight of a Masterpiece

As the art world converges on Lagos for the biennial, an unlikely issue is taking center stage: the environmental impact of collecting. Nigerian art collector and philanthropist, Eni Arose, has made waves by announcing that she will be carbon offsetting every flight she takes to attend auctions and exhibitions. Arose’s move has sparked a heated debate among collectors, curators, and artists about the responsibility that comes with buying and selling art.

item.title: First-time buyers hit as mortgage rates keep rising
item.description:
Market Meltdown: As Mortgage Rates Soar, First-Time Buyers Bear the Brunt

In a shocking turn of events, the UK mortgage market has witnessed a precipitous decline in deals for first-time buyers, a demographic that has long been the backbone of the country’s housing market. Over 200 deals have vanished since 6 March, leaving aspiring homeowners reeling as the specter of unaffordability looms large. As mortgage rates continue their upward trajectory, industry insiders warn of a perfect storm that threatens to upend the fragile balance of the UK’s housing market.

item.title: China’s Country Garden to post up to US$320 million profit after debt overhaul
item.description:
China’s Debt Odyssey: Country Garden’s Road to Recovery

As the sun set over the gleaming skyscrapers of Shenzhen, China’s southern technology hub, whispers of a once-faltering giant’s resurgence began to circulate among financial circles. Country Garden Holdings, one of the world’s largest property developers, is poised to post a profit of up to US$320 million for the year 2025, marking a remarkable turnaround from its US$35.15 billion loss just a year prior. The Hong Kong-listed company’s filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange on Monday night revealed a non-cash gain of approximately 1 billion yuan to 2.2 billion yuan, bolstered by the completion of its debt restructuring plan.

item.title: Cosmetics giant Estée Lauder in merger talks with owner of Jean Paul Gaultier and Rabanne
item.description:
Global Beauty Unites: Estée Lauder Pursues Merger with French Fashion House Owner

The cosmetics industry is on the cusp of a seismic shift as Estée Lauder Companies, a global giant in the beauty sector, is reportedly in advanced talks to merge with the parent company of Jean Paul Gaultier and Pierre Balmain’s successor, Spanish designer Paco Rabanne, among other luxury fashion brands. The proposed deal would catapult Estée Lauder to new heights, creating a behemoth with an unparalleled portfolio of beauty and fashion labels, including Tom Ford, Bobbi Brown, and the soon-to-be-integrated brands from the French fashion house owner. The merger talks have sent shockwaves through the industry, sparking both excitement and trepidation among investors, competitors, and analysts.

item.title: ‘Don’t Make Any Deal’: Trump Tells Republicans to Hold Firm on Shutdown Talks
item.description:
A Shutdown Stalemate

As night fell on the nation’s capital, the air was heavy with tension as the impasse over funding the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) stretched into its fourth week. The standoff, a byproduct of a contentious debate over voter ID legislation, has brought Washington to a virtual standstill, with lawmakers struggling to find common ground on a measure that has the potential to reshape the electoral landscape.

item.title: Australia politics live: NSW reveals laws to crush illegal ebikes; Kate Chaney pushes for action 1,000 days after gambling ad ban report
item.description:
Australia’s Ebike Crackdown and the Rise of AI Companions: A Perfect Storm

As the sun rises over the iconic Sydney Opera House, a new wave of legislation is set to sweep through the state of New South Wales, leaving a trail of uncertainty in its wake. On Tuesday, the state government will introduce laws that grant authorities unprecedented powers to seize high-powered e-motorbikes, a move aimed at combatting the growing scourge of illegal ebikes on the state’s roads. But as the dust settles on this significant development, a more insidious threat is emerging – one that has the potential to entrap and entrance the very minds of Australia’s children.

item.title: Far more countries face critical food insecurity if world heats up by 2C, analysis shows
item.description:
Uncharted Territory: Climate Change and the Fragility of Food Systems

A 2-degree Celsius rise in global temperatures is an existential threat to the food security of millions worldwide, with far-reaching consequences for low-income nations. The notion that some countries will be hit harder than others is not a new concept, but the stark reality is that the world’s most vulnerable regions are facing an unprecedented crisis. As the planet continues to warm, the delicate balance of food systems is under intense pressure, with the IIED’s analysis painting a dire picture of a future where the divide between rich and poor grows exponentially.

item.title: Benue university shut after students protest over NELFUND disbursements
item.description:
Nigeria’s Higher Education Imperiled by Funding Woes

Fists are clenched, banners held high, and chants pierce the air as hundreds of Benue State University students block the main gate, refusing to budge until their demands are met. The protest, which began in the early hours of the morning, has culminated in the university’s administration announcing its decision to shut down the institution, effective immediately. The catalyst for this unprecedented action lies at the intersection of government funding and student welfare, specifically the contentious handling of NELFUND disbursements.

item.title: For Western Oil Companies, War in Iran Means Bigger Profits, and Risks
item.description:
Western Oil Companies Face a Double-Edged Sword in Iran

A sudden escalation of tensions in the Middle East has sent shockwaves through the global energy market, with Western oil and gas companies poised to reap significant profits from the resulting surge in prices. However, beneath the surface of this windfall lies a complex web of risks and uncertainties that threaten to undermine the long-term sustainability of the sector. As the stakes rise, American and European companies are grappling with the implications of a potential war in Iran, a development that could reshape the global energy landscape forever.

item.title: National Guard in Hawaii assist after Oahu flood
item.description:
Catastrophic Waters

Darkness has descended upon the island of Oahu, where torrential rains have unleashed a deluge of biblical proportions. For days, the relentless downpour has pounded the parched earth, transforming the lush landscapes into a maelstrom of muddy waters and shattered dreams. As the floodwaters continue to rise, the people of Oahu are grappling with the worst flooding in two decades, leaving a trail of devastation in its wake.

item.title: How Epstein Helped Solve a Billionaire’s Problems With Women
item.description:
The Enigmatic Epstein Equation

Leon Black, the chairman and CEO of private equity firm Apollo Global Management, has been under increasing scrutiny for his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. While Epstein’s crimes have been well-documented, the extent of his involvement with Black, one of the world’s most influential billionaires, remains shrouded in mystery. A recent report reveals that Epstein received $170 million from Black for work that went far beyond tax and estate planning, raising serious questions about the nature of their relationship and the potential consequences for Black’s reputation and business empire.

item.title: Jeff Webb, Who Built a Competitive Cheerleading Empire, Dies at 76
item.description:
The Forgotten Father of Competitive Cheerleading

Jeff Webb, the enigmatic entrepreneur who built a global sports empire around the seemingly innocuous world of cheerleading, has passed away at the age of 76. Webb’s legacy is a testament to his unyielding vision and tireless efforts to professionalize a sport that was once viewed as a quaint, American pastime. At the helm of Varsity Spirit, the company he founded in 1974, Webb transformed cheerleading into a multibillion-dollar industry that has captivated audiences worldwide.

item.title: As Northwest Flooding Worsens, Conflicting Interests Stymie Solutions
item.description:
Catastrophic Convergence

A relentless deluge of rain pummels the parched landscape of Washington’s Northwest, unleashing a torrent of floodwaters that sweep across farmland, displace families, and imperil the livelihoods of those who depend on the region’s rich bounty. The sheer force of this tempest is nothing short of breathtaking: in mid-December, a record-breaking downpour shattered the previous mark set just four years prior, sending the already swollen rivers to catastrophic new heights. As the waters recede, a daunting question lingers: what will it take to prevent this calamity from becoming an annual occurrence, a grim harbinger of a climate future that refuses to yield?

item.title: Iran war threatens energy crisis worse than 1970s two oil shocks
item.description:
Global Oil Security Teeters on the Brink of Chaos

A flurry of airstrikes shook Tehran on Monday, sending shockwaves through the global energy market as the war in the Middle East rages on with no end in sight. The Israeli military’s fresh strikes on Iranian targets have reignited fears of a catastrophic energy crisis, one that could dwarf the impact of both the 1970s oil shocks combined. According to Fatih Birol, the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) executive director, the world is already losing oil at a rate that far exceeds the devastating effects of the 1970s oil embargo, the 1973 oil crisis, and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. As the global community struggles to contain the fallout from this escalating conflict, one thing is becoming increasingly clear: the future of global energy security hangs precariously in the balance.

item.title: Fearing Chaos of Climate Change, Some Seek Answers in Virtual Classroom
item.description:
Uncharted Territory

As the last remnants of a scorching Sahel summer dissipate, a group of 20 young climate scientists from sub-Saharan Africa convened on a virtual platform to tackle the most pressing question of their generation: how to navigate the uncharted territory of climate chaos. The monthlong seminar, convened by a non-profit think tank, aimed to equip this new generation of climate leaders with the knowledge and skills to anticipate and prepare for the mounting disruptions of global warming. For these young minds, the stakes are personal – their families, their communities, and their livelihoods hang precariously in the balance.

item.title: Stocks Tumble as Oil Prices Rise
item.description: As the global economy teeters on the precipice of a potentially catastrophic downturn, investors are facing a daunting reality: the war in the Middle East shows no signs of abating, and with it, the price of oil continues to skyrocket. The consequences are already being felt, with stocks tumbling in a fourth consecutive week of market turmoil. The situation is particularly dire for the world’s developing economies, which are heavily reliant on imported oil to fuel their growth.

item.title: Iran War Live Updates: Power Outages Are Reported in Tehran as Israel Launches Strikes
item.description:
A City in the Dark

The city of Tehran was plunged into chaos late last night as a wave of airstrikes rocked the Iranian capital, leaving residents without power and scrambling for safety. Eyewitness accounts describe a scene of utter destruction, with buildings reduced to rubble and the once-familiar skyline now shrouded in a thick layer of smoke. As the international community reels from the sudden escalation of tensions, one question dominates the conversation: what prompted Israel to launch such a brazen attack on a civilian target?

item.title: Courts’ Fight Over ‘Cop City’ Protests Raises Questions About Terrorism Laws and Environmental Activism
item.description:
Uncharted Territory

A makeshift memorial stands outside the former site of the South River Forest, a 85-acre woodland in Atlanta’s DeKalb County that’s been at the epicenter of a contentious land dispute. The trees have been cleared to make way for the construction of the Atlanta Police Foundation’s ‘Cop City,’ a $90 million training facility that’s been met with fierce resistance from environmental activists and community groups. The controversy has spilled into the courtroom, where a recent hearing raised questions about the limits of terrorism laws and the future of environmental activism in the United States.

item.title: Heat pumps work for me - but they're not yet a money saver
item.description:
A Flicker of Hope, a Sea of Uncertainty

As Emma Jenkins stood in her newly installed heat pump system, she couldn’t help but feel a sense of pride and accomplishment. The warm air circulating through her home was not only a testament to her commitment to reducing her carbon footprint, but also a beacon of hope for a more sustainable future. However, as she gazed at her energy bills, her enthusiasm began to wane. Despite the government’s push for Britons to transition to heat pumps, the financial reality for the average user remains a far cry from the oft-quoted eco-friendly rhetoric.

item.title: Changes to Hong Kong’s HK$2 transport subsidy scheme to kick in on April 3
item.description:
Transportation Divide in Hong Kong: A Tale of Two Cities

As the sun rises over Victoria Harbour on any given morning, the bustling streets of Hong Kong are alive with the hum of traffic, the chatter of pedestrians, and the gentle chime of tram bells. But beneath the surface of this cosmopolitan metropolis lies a tale of two cities – one for the haves and one for the have-nots. The recent announcement by the Hong Kong government to revise the city’s HK$2 transport subsidy scheme has left many questioning the very fabric of this city’s social contract. Effective next Friday, April 3, the subsidized rate will only apply to journeys costing HK$10 or less, leaving many elderly and disabled residents to bear the brunt of rising transport costs.

item.title: After Cosmic Crisp, Scientists Unveil an Apple for the Climate Change Era
item.description:
The Apple of Resilience

As the world’s farmers and consumers struggle to come to terms with the ever-more-reliable specter of unpredictable weather, a team of agronomists at Washington State University has unveiled a game-changing innovation in the realm of horticulture: the Sunflare apple. This latest addition to the apple family boasts a taste profile reminiscent of the hit Cosmic Crisp, but with a crucial twist - it has been engineered to withstand even the most extreme fluctuations in temperature and precipitation. For the millions of people around the world who rely on their local apple crops for sustenance and livelihood, the Sunflare represents a beacon of hope in a climate-changed world.

item.title: U.N. Climate Report Finds Growing Energy Imbalance on Earth
item.description:
A Tipping Point of Unmitigated Consequences

As the world’s leading climate scientists gather in Geneva, the United Nations’ latest report on the global energy balance delivers a stark reminder that the consequences of humanity’s addiction to fossil fuels are no longer a distant threat, but a palpable reality. The findings, based on decades of data analysis and cutting-edge research, paint a picture of a planet on a precipice, where the natural systems that have maintained equilibrium for millennia are now teetering on the verge of collapse. The report’s central message is clear: the continued burning of fossil fuels is locking heat in the Earth’s atmosphere, oceans, and land, effectively stranding it in a state of perpetual warming.

item.title: Asia stocks slide as US and Iran threaten to intensify war
item.description:
Global Markets on Edge as Tensions Escalate

Panic is spreading through the financial markets like wildfire, fueled by the latest developments in the simmering conflict between the United States and Iran. The US has been ratcheting up pressure on Tehran in recent weeks, with the imposition of fresh sanctions and the deployment of additional military assets to the region. Meanwhile, Iran has been steadily increasing its military presence in the Gulf, sparking fears of a potentially catastrophic war that could have far-reaching consequences for the global economy.

item.title: Australia politics live: Taylor targets PM over fuel ship cancellations as question time returns
item.description:
A Perfect Storm: Australia’s Petrol Crisis Amidst Global Tensions

As the Australian federal parliament reconvened in Canberra, the air was thick with tension as lawmakers clashed over the worsening petrol crisis. The Labor government, already under fire for its handling of the fuel shortage, faced pointed questions from the opposition, with key figures from both sides of the aisle trading barbs in a heated question time session. Amidst the domestic drama, international events are converging to create a perfect storm that threatens to further exacerbate the crisis.

item.title: Iran War Live Updates: Trump Uninterested in Cease-Fire Because U.S. Is ‘Obliterating the Other Side’
item.description: Tensions between the United States and Iran have reached a boiling point, with the conflict escalating into a full-blown crisis that has sent shockwaves across the globe. The price of oil remains stubbornly high, a stark reminder of the economic implications of this war. As the conflict rages on, the world watches with bated breath, wondering what the future holds for the region and the global economy. The United States, backed by its ally Israel, has been bombarding Iran with airstrikes, targeting key energy infrastructure, including oil refineries and natural gas fields. The Iranian government, on the other hand, has vowed to retaliate, threatening to unleash its military might on its enemies.

item.title: Nigeria: Who Makes the Best Jollof Rice? King Charles Offers 'Diplomatic' Answer
item.description: As the soft glow of candelabras danced across the opulent dining hall, a subtle yet palpable sense of cultural exchange filled the air at the state banquet in Windsor, where King Charles III played host to a distinguished gathering of Nigerian dignitaries. With the weight of diplomatic propriety momentarily set aside, the British monarch endeavored to find common ground with his esteemed guests, and in doing so, he casually dropped a reference to a dish that has long been a staple of West African cuisine: Jollof Rice. The remark, though lighthearted in tone, served as a testament to the profound impact that Nigerians have had on various aspects of British society, from the culinary scene to the realms of politics, arts, and culture.

item.title: Missile fire kills three Palestinians in occupied West Bank
item.description: Violence has once again erupted in the occupied West Bank, leaving a trail of death and destruction in its wake. The latest incident, which occurred on Wednesday night, saw missile fragments strike a hair salon near Hebron, resulting in the loss of three lives and injuring 13 others. The victims, who included a teenager, were caught off guard by the sudden and devastating attack, which has sent shockwaves throughout the Palestinian community. As the people of the West Bank struggle to come to terms with this latest tragedy, questions are being raised about the circumstances surrounding the attack and the ongoing struggle for peace and security in the region.

item.title: Qatar contains two Ras Laffan fires, third still burning
item.description: Fierce blazes have ravaged the Ras Laffan Industrial Area in Qatar, with two of the three fires now under control, according to a statement released by the country’s interior ministry. The swift response by civil defence teams has been credited with containing the fires, preventing any reported injuries and potentially mitigating the damage to the industrial facilities. As the embers of the two extinguished fires continue to smoulder, attention has turned to the third fire, which remains active and poses a persistent threat to the area.

item.title: Ship struck by 'unknown projectile' near Qatar's Ras Laffan
item.description: Ras Laffan, a bustling industrial hub on Qatar’s northeastern coast, is abuzz with activity as the world’s energy giants converge to tap into the region’s vast natural gas reserves. But beneath the surface of this economic powerhouse, tensions are simmering, and the latest incident to rock the waters off Ras Laffan has sent shockwaves throughout the maritime community. A vessel operating in the area has been struck by an “unknown projectile,” sparking fears of a potential escalation in the region’s volatile security landscape.

item.title: Retired Belgian Diplomat, 93, Faces Trial Over 1961 Killing of Congolese Leader
item.description: Diplomatic immunity, a concept once thought to be inviolable, has been pierced by a Brussels court’s groundbreaking decision to put a 93-year-old retired Belgian diplomat on trial for his alleged role in the 1961 assassination of Patrice Lumumba, the Democratic Republic of Congo’s first prime minister. This development has sent shockwaves through the international community, sparking a mixture of astonishment and curiosity about the events that led to this moment. The trial promises to shed new light on a dark chapter in Belgian-Congolese relations, one that has haunted the conscience of both nations for decades. As the world watches, the forthcoming trial will not only seek to establish the truth behind Lumumba’s tragic death but also serve as a test of the reach of international law and the accountability of those who have long been shielded by their diplomatic status.

item.title: Saudi analyst says kingdom will activate defence pact with Pakistan if it joins Iran war
item.description: As the conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran continues to escalate, the possibility of Saudi Arabia joining the fray has become a pressing concern for nations across the globe. The kingdom’s potential involvement in the war has significant implications, particularly in light of its mutual defence pact with Pakistan, which was signed last year. This agreement has raised eyebrows among geopolitical observers, as it could potentially draw Pakistan into the conflict and even put its nuclear arsenal on the table.

item.title: NSIA signs MoU with UK firm to develop dairy livestock platform in Nigeria
item.description: Dairy farming in Nigeria is on the cusp of a significant transformation, as the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, NSIA, has signed a memorandum of understanding with a UK-based firm to develop a state-of-the-art dairy livestock platform in the country. This ambitious project has the potential to revolutionize the Nigerian dairy industry, which has long been plagued by low milk yields, limited access to quality feed, and inadequate infrastructure. The partnership is expected to bring in much-needed investment, expertise, and technology to boost the sector, with far-reaching implications for the country’s food security, economy, and employment landscape.

item.title: Senegal govt alleges corruption in decision to hand AFCON title to Morocco
item.description: Climate change is exacerbating the already precarious living conditions of millions of people in West Africa, where rising temperatures and altered precipitation patterns are affecting agricultural productivity, food security, and human health. The region’s vulnerability to climate-related shocks is further compounded by limited economic resources, inadequate infrastructure, and weak institutional capacity. As the international community grapples with the challenges of mitigating and adapting to climate change, the human and economic impact of this global phenomenon on West Africa’s most vulnerable populations demands urgent attention. The recent controversy surrounding the African Cup of Nations, which saw Senegal stripped of the title after a mid-final protest, has highlighted the complexities of climate change, corruption, and sports in the region.

item.title: Average age of first time buyer climbs to 34
item.description: Rising property prices, stagnating wages, and shifting demographics have combined to create a formidable barrier for young people seeking to enter the housing market, with the average age of first-time buyers now standing at 34, a staggering eight years higher than it was just two decades ago. This stark reality is the central finding of a comprehensive new report that examines the evolving landscape of homeownership, highlighting the profound implications for individuals, communities, and the broader economy. As the dream of homeownership becomes increasingly elusive for many, the consequences of this trend are being felt far beyond the realm of personal finance, with significant social and economic repercussions that will be felt for generations to come.

item.title: Red Sea fix? China-bound oil tankers tap Saudi plan to bypass Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Saudi Arabia’s decision to activate its Red Sea “Plan B” has sent ripples across the global energy landscape, as the kingdom seeks to divert crude oil exports away from the increasingly volatile Strait of Hormuz. The move is aimed at ensuring the uninterrupted flow of oil to key markets, particularly China, which is the world’s largest crude oil importer. By rerouting tankers, including Chinese very large crude carriers (VLCCs), through the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia is attempting to mitigate the risks associated with the strategic waterway, which has been at the center of escalating tensions between Iran, the United States, and Israel.

item.title: Who blinks first: What Iran’s Strait of Hormuz strategy reveals about its war goals
item.description: Tensions in the Strait of Hormuz have reached a boiling point, with a series of attacks on ships and strikes across the region exposing the complex and calculated strategy of Iran’s war goals. As the world watches with bated breath, the question on everyone’s mind is: who will blink first? The answer, much like the waters of the Strait itself, is murky and fraught with uncertainty. With the United States, Israel, and Gulf states locked in a high-stakes game of cat and mouse with Tehran, the region teeters on the brink of all-out war. The consequences of such a conflict would be catastrophic, with far-reaching implications for global security, trade, and the balance of power in the Middle East.

item.title: Sudan: RSF reportedly take over town near Chadian border
item.description: Sudan’s fragile security landscape has been further destabilized by the reported seizure of the border town of Al-Tina in North Darfur State by fighters from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. This development comes as fighting intensifies across the country’s west, raising concerns about the potential for regional instability and the impact on civilians. The images of RSF fighters celebrating their apparent victory, firing in the air and brandishing weapons, have sent shockwaves through the region, with many fearing the consequences of this escalation.

item.title: Israeli gas strike 'carried out with US support and approval'
item.description: As flames engulfed the largest natural gas site in Iran, a senior Israeli official revealed that the devastating attack was carried out with the full support and approval of the United States. This startling admission has sent shockwaves across the globe, exposing the intricate web of alliances and rivalries that shape the complex geopolitics of the Middle East. The Israeli official’s claim, corroborated by Israeli journalist Barak Ravid, has significant implications for the region, where the delicate balance of power is increasingly being tested by the actions of major world powers.

item.title: The Drum Major Is Gone: A Tribute to Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson
item.description: There are people who arrive in the world as if they were sent with a specific assignment. They do not drift through history — they shape it. They do not ask permission to speak — they thunder. Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson was one of those people. Born October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, a city that taught him injustice before it taught him anything else, he left this world on February 17, 2026, at the age of 84 — peacefully, surrounded by family, in Chicago, the city he made his pulpit and his battlefield.
